[MATH: \lim_{x\to3}\log_2{x} = \log_2{3}\approx 1.58.]

Content:
For logarithmic functions, the limit at a point is equal to the value of the function at that point, so for any base [MATH: b \gt 1] we have

items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's take a look again at the function [MATH: y=\log_2(x).]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/63aca78cdf8a6e3c36e5f58b1749d9a4]

Content:
As [MATH: x] gets larger and larger, the curve increases without bound. So, we have

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{x\to\infty} \log_2{x}= \infty.]

Content:
The curve is not defined for [MATH: x\leq 0,] but as [MATH: x] approaches zero from the right the curve decreases without bound. So

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{x\to0^+}\log_2{x} = -\infty.]

Content:
Also, note that

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{x\to0^-}\log_2{x} = \textrm{DNE},\qquad\qquad \lim_{x\to0}\log_2{x} = \textrm{DNE}.]

Content:
These properties are true for logarithms of any base [MATH: b\gt 1.]

sections.normalized_html:
Let's sketch the graph of [MATH: y = \ln(x+2).]

The function is not defined for [MATH: x\leq -2.] Therefore,

[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to (-2)^{-}} \ln (x+2) = \textrm{DNE}.]

However, the function is defined for [MATH: x\gt -2.] Therefore,

[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to (-2)^{+}} \ln (x+2) = -\infty.]

sections.normalized_html:
Let's sketch the graph of [MATH: y = \ln(x-2).]

The function is not defined for [MATH: x\leq 2.] Therefore,

[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to 2^{-}} \ln (x-2) = \textrm{DNE}.]

However, the function is defined for [MATH: x\gt 2.] Therefore,

[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to 2^{+}} \ln (x-2) = -\infty.]

Since the left and right-sided limits are not equal, we have [MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to 2} \ln (x-2) = \textrm{DNE}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let's look at the graph of [MATH: y=\log_2{x}] below.

Graphic:

Content:
From the graph, we see that

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{x\to3}\log_2{x} = \log_2{3}\approx 1.58.]

Content:
For logarithmic functions, the limit at a point is equal to the value of the function at that point, so for any base [MATH: b \gt 1] we have

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{x\to c}\log_b{x} = \log_b{c}.]

Content:
Remember that logarithms are only defined for positive inputs [MATH: x\gt 0,] so we must have [MATH: c>0.] Otherwise, the limit does not exist [MATH: \textrm{(DNE}).]

Item 2 — Example: Evaluating Using Direct Substitution

To find this limit, we substitute [MATH: x=4] into the expression:

[MATH: lim_(x → 4)\log_{2} (x + 4)|= \log_{2} (4 + 4); = \log_{2} (8); = \log_{2} (2^{3}); = 3]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Infinite Limits and Limits at Infinity of Logarithmic Functions

Content:
Let's take a look again at the function [MATH: y=\log_2(x).]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/63aca78cdf8a6e3c36e5f58b1749d9a4]

Content:
As [MATH: x] gets larger and larger, the curve increases without bound. So, we have

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{x\to\infty} \log_2{x}= \infty.]

Content:
The curve is not defined for [MATH: x\leq 0,] but as [MATH: x] approaches zero from the right the curve decreases without bound. So

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{x\to0^+}\log_2{x} = -\infty.]

Content:
Also, note that

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{x\to0^-}\log_2{x} = \textrm{DNE},\qquad\qquad \lim_{x\to0}\log_2{x} = \textrm{DNE}.]

Content:
These properties are true for logarithms of any base [MATH: b\gt 1.]
